title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing — September 17, 2026 (Chile Skips a 35-Year Tradition, and a Year-Old Hospital Decision Tests a Sourcing Bar)
headline: Chile skipped its dictatorship-anniversary commemoration for the first time since 1990.
summary:
Ten organizations were reviewed overnight, and two more rows were checked only for screening. Not one published score changed, and no new downgrade or upgrade was filed.

Chile's government held no official commemoration of the 1973-1990 dictatorship's victims this year, the first time since democracy returned in 1990. Measuring that decision alongside the rest of Chile's record produced a score of 41.9 out of 100, well below its published 62.5. That finding matches a downgrade proposal already open since 1 September, so no second filing was made. Chile's published score is unchanged.

Diligent Robotics has never been individually assessed before. This cycle's first review found an older story. A Washington hospital system, MultiCare, ended a contract for 14 of the company's delivery robots roughly a year earlier, around early 2025. It cited cost against how little the robots were used, according to a regional newspaper report from February 2026 and a nurses' union statement from March 2026. Measuring that finding alone would move Diligent Robotics out of the benchmark's top tier. The finding was set aside instead, for two reasons. The two sources located fall short of this benchmark's two-source, one-top-tier bar for a band-change finding. And the crossing depends on a scoring bonus threshold in a score never individually checked before. Diligent Robotics' published score of 83.0 is unchanged. Separately, the AI lab Imbue confirmed its own top-tier score this cycle — published 81.4, measured 81.1. Seven of its eight categories sit exactly at that same threshold.

The United Nations' human rights chief said 23 people have died in United States immigration custody so far in 2026, and separately warned that a reported plan to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves would increase the violence associated with their operations. Neither fact moved the score. The deaths continue a pattern already counted in a June downgrade, and a plan is not scored until it happens. The United States' published score of 17.5, in the benchmark's lowest band, is unchanged.

Bolivia's legislature approved a 90-day extension of the government's state of emergency. Starbucks lost part of a federal appeals case over an illegal threat to a pregnant worker's maternity benefits, a finding that matches a downgrade Starbucks already has open. An immigration agency's plan to buy robot dogs from Boston Dynamics remains a forecast with no contract signed. Romania's government faced a livestock farmers' protest over a live-export ban that belongs to the European Commission, not Romania. And Harmonic Bionics' published score still describes a robotics business that another company bought in 2025.

pipeline.rosterNote: The roster held at 1,329 entities this cycle. Coverage combined seven scanner-flagged organizations with five rotation-backfill organizations that had never been individually reviewed before.
pipeline.queueHandling: Twelve organizations were reviewed. Ten were scored, and none produced a new proposal: seven scores were confirmed unchanged, two measurements matched proposals already open since 1 September without duplicating them, and one measurement found a boundary crossing that fell short of this benchmark's sourcing bar for a public finding. Two rows were reviewed for screening only. An immigration agency's robot-purchase plan attaches to no scored conduct on the row it was flagged against, and one row was set aside under an open question about three different published scores describing what may be the same underlying company. No published ranking changed.

topSignals.title: Chile Skips Its Dictatorship Commemoration for the First Time Since 1990
topSignals.whyItMatters: The government broke a 35-year tradition of marking the coup anniversary. A measurement of that decision matches a downgrade already under review, and the published score has not moved.
topSignals.description:
On 11 September 2026, the anniversary of the 1973 coup, Chile's government under President Jose Antonio Kast held no official commemoration for the victims of the 1973-1990 dictatorship — the first time since democracy returned in 1990. Police also detained 284 people that day and the day before, including 31 minors, as protesters clashed with police; the country's own Security Minister reported 34 percent fewer violent incidents than in 2025 alongside 80 percent more detentions.

Measuring Chile's record against this evidence, including one subdimension move for the missing commemoration, produces a score of 41.9 out of 100 — well below the published 62.5, and low enough to cross out of the benchmark's Established band into Functional. That finding was not filed as a new proposal. It reproduces, within normal rounding, a downgrade already proposed on 1 September and still under review, so filing a second one would have duplicated the same open finding. Chile's published score remains 62.5.

evidence.claim: Civil society groups describe a pattern of "silent dismantling" affecting Chile's transitional-justice institutions under the new government — an allegation, not an independently confirmed finding.
evidence.source: Columbia Global Freedom of Expression Protest Monitor

topSignals.title: A Hospital's Year-Old Decision to Drop Delivery Robots Falls Short of a Sourcing Bar
topSignals.whyItMatters: A Washington hospital dropped its Diligent robots about a year ago, found during the company's first review. The finding fell short on sourcing, and the crossing rests on a threshold never checked before.
topSignals.description:
Diligent Robotics has never been individually assessed before. This cycle's first review turned up an older story. MultiCare, a Washington state hospital system, bought 14 Moxi delivery robots from Diligent Robotics starting in 2023. It ended the contract about a year before February 2026, around early 2025, saying the cost did not justify how little the robots were used. A regional newspaper reported the story on 17 February 2026, and the hospital's nurses' union added its own account on 13 March 2026. The union, the Washington State Nurses Association, said the robots needed escorts between floors and never delivered meaningful time savings. It also said nurses had no voice in the original purchasing decision. Diligent Robotics still reports nearly 100 robots operating in more than 25 hospital facilities, using its own activity counts; no independent outcome evaluation was located.

Measuring this evidence against Diligent Robotics' published, never-individually-checked score of 83.0 produces 79.8 — enough to cross out of the Exemplary band into Established. That finding was set aside for two reasons. This benchmark requires at least two independent sources before publishing a band-change finding, with one of them top-tier. The evidence located here — a regional news report and a nurses' union statement — does not include a top-tier source. The crossing also depends on a scoring bonus that disappears once enough categories fall below an exact threshold, in a score that had never been checked against evidence before. Diligent Robotics' published score of 83.0 is unchanged.

Separately, the AI lab Imbue confirmed its own published score of 81.4 this cycle, measured at 81.1, with no independent evidence located in either direction. Its Exemplary rating rests on seven of eight categories sitting at exactly the scoring formula's bonus threshold — the same structural pattern now visible in Diligent Robotics' case. Both are referred to a joint review of every organization whose top-tier score depends on that threshold.

evidence.claim: The nurses' union said staff had no voice at the table when the hospital decided to buy the Moxi robots it later removed, citing cost against how little they were used.

topSignals.title: United Nations Human Rights Chief Says 23 Have Died in US Immigration Custody This Year
topSignals.whyItMatters: The death count keeps climbing, but it continues a pattern already priced into a June downgrade. A reported plan for electric shock gloves is not scored unless it actually happens.
topSignals.description:
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk told the Human Rights Council on 7 September 2026 that four more people had died in United States immigration custody since June, bringing the total to 23 deaths in 2026. He demanded accountability and separately raised alarm at reports that the Department of Homeland Security is seeking to spend $10 million to $20 million on electric shock gloves for immigration agents, warning the devices would increase the violence associated with their operations.

A rising death count from an official United Nations statement is treated as a continuing pattern, not a new finding, because it was already built into a downgrade applied in June 2026. The shock-glove purchase is a reported procurement plan; nothing has been bought or deployed on the public record. Measuring both facts together produces 16.3 out of 100, within normal rounding of the published 17.5. The United States' published score of 17.5, in the benchmark's lowest band, is unchanged.

evidence.quote: increase the violence associated with their operations
evidence.claim: The UN human rights chief warned that equipping US immigration agents with electric shock gloves would increase the violence associated with their operations.
evidence.source: Euronews, quoting UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk

evidence.claim: The Department of Homeland Security described the shock gloves it is reportedly seeking to buy as "distraction and de-escalation" tools.

topSignals.title: A Federal Appeals Court Upholds One Unlawful Threat Against a Pregnant Starbucks Worker
topSignals.whyItMatters: Judges threw out most of a union-related case but kept one finding: Starbucks illegally threatened a pregnant worker's maternity benefits. The finding matches a downgrade already under review.
topSignals.description:
On 4 September 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit refused to enforce most of a National Labor Relations Board ruling against a Starbucks store in Wichita, Kansas, rejecting findings that the company cut hours and closed a hiring portal because of union activity. The court did uphold one finding: that a Starbucks manager illegally threatened to deny maternity leave benefits to a pregnant employee if her store unionized.

Measuring this mixed ruling against Starbucks' record produces 43.1 out of 100, matching a downgrade proposal already open since 1 September to the decimal point. No second finding was filed. Starbucks' published score of 48.4 is unchanged.

topSignals.title: Bolivia's Legislature Approves a 90-Day Extension of Emergency Powers
topSignals.whyItMatters: The extension continues emergency rule already reflected in Bolivia's score. An undeclared state-of-siege option is not counted unless it is actually used.
topSignals.description:
Bolivia's executive approved a 90-day extension of the country's state of exception on 14 September 2026, and the Legislative Assembly ratified it on 17 September with 100 of 158 members voting in favor after a nine-hour session. A government spokesperson said further measures, including a possible state of siege with curfews, would be imposed if the government judged it necessary — an option the decree allows but that has not been used.

The extension continues an emergency regime already reflected in Bolivia's published score; it does not add a new category of harm, and a contemplated-but-undeclared measure is not scored as conduct. Measuring the extension against Bolivia's record produces 5.0 out of 100, within normal rounding of the published 6.3. Bolivia's published score is unchanged.

evidence.quote: Si se ve pertinente imponer otras medidas, lo vamos a hacer, la ley lo contempla
evidence.claim: A government spokesperson said further measures, including a possible state of siege, would be imposed "if deemed pertinent," since the law allows it — a statement short of an actual declaration.

topSignals.title: Harmonic Bionics' Published Score Still Describes a Business Sold in 2025
topSignals.whyItMatters: Another company bought Harmonic Bionics' assets and business more than a year ago. The published row has not caught up, and its score sits close to a lower band.
topSignals.description:
Bioness Medical announced on 18 June 2025 that it had acquired the assets and business of Harmonic Bionics, maker of the Harmony SHR upper-limb rehabilitation exoskeleton. The published robotics-labs row still describes the business under its original name; how the row should reflect the acquisition is an open question, not resolved by this cycle.

An FDA adverse-event report on file describes a February 2024 malfunction during a product demonstration, in which an emergency stop was engaged and smoke was seen in a rear enclosure; no patient was present, and the manufacturer retrieved the part and alerted other customers. That response supports the transparency the published score already credits. Measuring the full record produces 60.6 out of 100, within normal rounding of the published 62.5 — just 0.6 points above the boundary with the benchmark's Functional band. Harmonic Bionics' published score is unchanged.

topSignals.title: Romanian Farmers Clash With Police Over an Export Ban That Belongs to Brussels, Not Bucharest
topSignals.whyItMatters: About 2,000 livestock farmers protested a live-export ban imposed by the European Commission, not Romania's government. Romania's own response is what the benchmark actually scores.
topSignals.description:
About 2,000 livestock farmers protested outside Romania's government building in Bucharest on 15 September 2026 over the handling of animal-disease outbreaks and a resulting halt to live-sheep exports. Gendarmes used tear gas after protesters broke through a security cordon and threw objects at officers; 26 people were detained and about 24 injured, including 8 gendarmes, according to Agence France-Presse.

The live-export ban itself was imposed by the European Commission, not Romania's government, and is not scored as Romanian conduct. What is scored is Romania's own response: the government's statement described the protest as having degenerated into regrettable acts of violence, without addressing the gendarmerie's tear-gas use, and a promised drought-compensation payment was cut from 100 to 19 euros per hectare. Measuring this record produces 35.6 out of 100, within normal rounding of the published 37.5. Romania's published score is unchanged.

evidence.quote: broke through security cordons and threw objects at officers
evidence.claim: Gendarmes used tear gas after protesting farmers broke through security cordons and threw objects at officers in Bucharest.

evidence.quote: degenerated into regrettable acts of violence
evidence.claim: Romania's government described the protest as having degenerated into regrettable acts of violence, without addressing the gendarmerie's own tear-gas use.
evidence.source: France 24 (AFP), quoting a Romanian government statement

topSignals.title: An Immigration Agency's Robot-Dog Purchase Is Still Just a Plan
topSignals.whyItMatters: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement wants to spend up to $2 million on Boston Dynamics' Spot robots. No contract has been signed, so nothing was scored for either the robot or the company.
topSignals.description:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement is reportedly planning to spend up to $2 million on Boston Dynamics' Spot robots for inspection and hazard-assessment work, with an expected solicitation as early as 4 September 2026. As of 9 September, no request for proposals had been issued and no contract had been signed. Boston Dynamics restated its standing policy that any attempted weaponization of its robots is strictly prohibited, and that law-enforcement customers must adopt a public use policy before deployment — terms the company applies to every customer.

A government agency's purchase plan is not conduct by the robot maker, and restating an existing policy is not new conduct either. No evidence supports a change in either direction, on this row or on Boston Dynamics' own company score. Nothing was scored, and this row's published figure is unchanged.

evidence.quote: the government has not yet issued an RFP for this.
evidence.claim: As of 9 September 2026, the federal government had not yet issued a request for proposals for the reported Spot-robot purchase.

evidence.quote: any attempted weaponization of Boston Dynamics' robots is strictly prohibited
evidence.claim: Boston Dynamics restated its standing policy that any attempted weaponization of its robots is strictly prohibited, regardless of the customer.

methodologyNotes.name: A Scoring Bonus Can Disappear Even With No Conduct Change
methodologyNotes.description: Diligent Robotics and Imbue both show how the benchmark's scoring formula behaves near its own bonus threshold. Organizations earn a bonus of up to 10 points for scoring at or above a set line (4.0 out of 5) across all eight of the benchmark's categories. That bonus is gone entirely once five of the eight categories fall below the line, and shrinks by a fifth for each category below it in between. Diligent Robotics' single evidence-based category move was enough to cross that line for one category, which is why a comparatively small change in the underlying evidence produced a large change in the measured score. Imbue's published score depends on the same threshold with no evidence in either direction located this cycle.

methodologyNotes.name: Why a Measured Band Crossing Does Not Always Become a Public Finding
methodologyNotes.description: Before this benchmark publishes a finding that would move an organization across a band boundary, it requires at least two independent sources, with at least one at the benchmark's top evidence tier. Diligent Robotics' measurement this cycle crossed a band boundary on the evidence located, but that evidence — a union statement and a regional news report — did not include a top-tier source, so the finding was set aside rather than published. Chile's measurement corroborated a boundary crossing already under review from a proposal filed on 1 September, so it was recorded as supporting evidence rather than a second, duplicate finding.
